activities.title: Landscape and System Inventory
activities.narrationTitle: Day One — I Start the Engagement
activities.narration: I begin by meeting with the executive sponsor to understand what management expects from the controls review, the concerns they want addressed, the people who will participate, and how unresolved matters should be escalated. I then meet with the Head of IT Applications to begin understanding the client's technology environment. I ask for the Landscape Diagram and System List, the Hosting and Data-Centre Details, and any other existing documents that explain the environment. I use this information to begin building the Landscape and System Inventory.
reviewQuestions: What did you identify correctly?
What did you miss?
Did you record anything without proof?
What should remain outstanding?
What would you ask next?
Who would you ask?

connect.nowKnow: The systems and components that support the client's environment.
connect.stillNeed: How important business information enters, leaves and moves between systems.

Module 1 — Taking Command of the Controls Project
activities.narration:
It is Monday morning and I am now accountable for the controls project. My first mistake would be to start doing the team's work. Before I change anything, I need to understand what I have inherited.

I begin with the sponsor. I confirm why the project exists, what management expects, what deadlines cannot move, what concerns already exist and which decisions are waiting for me. I do not accept a green status simply because someone tells me the project is green. I ask what evidence supports the status.

Next I meet the team. I want to know who owns each workstream, what each person is working on, what is overdue, what is blocked and where the team believes the greatest risks are. I compare those answers with the project plan, the fourteen foundation artifacts, prior audit findings and the current evidence requests.

By the end of the first few days I should be able to separate four things: what is confirmed, what is incomplete, what is at risk and what requires a management decision. I am not trying to solve every problem myself. I am establishing control of the work.

By Friday I prepare my first management status. It tells the sponsor what I know, what I do not yet know, the immediate risks, the overdue items, the people responsible and the decisions I need. That is how I begin leading the controls project.
reviewQuestions: What must I know before changing the inherited project?
Which facts are confirmed and which are still assumptions?
What are the three most urgent risks?
What should I personally own and what should I delegate?
What must be in Friday's sponsor status?

connect.nowKnow: I understand what I inherited and what management expects.
connect.stillNeed: I still need a delivery model that makes ownership and accountability explicit.
connect.buildNext: Build the team RACI and resource plan.

activities.scenario: Monday, 8:30 AM. You have just been appointed Controls Lead. The project is already underway. Your sponsor wants a reliable status assessment by Friday. You inherit incomplete workbooks, unresolved audit requests, prior findings and a team whose responsibilities are unclear.
activities.purpose: Move from project participant to accountable Controls Lead. Establish control of scope, people, deadlines, inherited artifacts, audit commitments and immediate risks.

activities.title: Module 2 — Building and Managing the Controls Team
activities.narration:
I already know how the controls artifacts are built. My job now is to make sure the right people build them at the right time and to the right standard.

I start with the deliverables, not with people's job titles. For each artifact I identify who is responsible for preparing it, who is accountable for accepting it, who must be consulted and who needs to be informed. I then look at effort, dependencies and deadlines.

I do not delegate vaguely. I define the expected output, the source information, the due date, the review criteria and the point at which the person must escalate a problem. If an analyst owns the Risk Register, that does not mean I have abandoned the Risk Register. It means the analyst prepares it and I remain accountable for its quality.

I also protect specialist time. The SAP Security specialist should not be used for administrative work that an analyst can perform. I use specialists where technical judgment is needed and analysts where structured evidence gathering, documentation and testing can be performed under supervision.

The result is a delivery model in which everyone knows what they own, what good looks like, when I will review it and what happens when the work falls behind.
sourceDocuments: Team RACI and Resource Delivery Plan
activities.completedWorkbook: Team RACI and Resource Delivery Plan
reviewQuestions: Is every deliverable assigned to one responsible owner?
Is accountability clear even where preparation is delegated?
Are specialist resources being used for specialist work?
What dependencies could delay delivery?
Where are the review and escalation gates?

connect.nowKnow: I know who owns each deliverable and how the team will work.
connect.stillNeed: I still need a reliable method to judge the quality of work produced by others.
connect.buildNext: Learn the Controls Lead QA review method.

activities.title: Module 3 — Reviewing and Approving Team Work
activities.narration:
A document can look complete and still be wrong. As Controls Lead, I need a repeatable way to review other people's work.

I begin with completeness. Are the required fields, owners, populations, periods and conclusions present? Then I test accuracy. Does the work agree with the source evidence?

Next I ask whether important statements are supported. If the workpaper says a quarterly review occurred, I need evidence that the review occurred for the correct quarter and population. I then check traceability. Can I move from the scoped process to the risk, from the risk to the control, from the control to the owner and evidence, and from the evidence to the test and conclusion?

I check whether the control really addresses the risk. I check whether the evidence is sufficient and reliable. I check whether the test procedure actually proves the control objective. Finally, I ask whether the conclusion is defensible.

My choices are not simply pass or fail. I can approve the work, return it for correction, request more evidence or escalate an issue. The goal is not to redo the analyst's work. The goal is to know when the work is good enough to stand behind.
sourceDocuments: Controls Lead QA Review Checklist and Review Notes
activities.completedWorkbook: Controls Lead QA Review Checklist and Review Notes
reviewQuestions: Is the work complete?
Is it accurate and supported?
Can I trace risk to control to evidence to test to conclusion?
Would I defend this work to an auditor?
Approve, return, request evidence or escalate — and why?

connect.nowKnow: I can review controls work without reperforming all of it.
connect.stillNeed: I still need enough SAP technical literacy to challenge specialists intelligently.

activities.title: Module 4 — SAP Technical Literacy for Controls Leaders
activities.narration:
I do not need to become the SAP Security administrator, Basis engineer or functional configurator. I do need enough technical understanding to recognize when an answer is incomplete.

For the landscape, I need to know which systems support the in-scope processes and where responsibility changes between the company, SAP and other providers. For access, I need to understand the user lifecycle, roles, approvals, privileged access and how access is removed.

For GRC, I need to understand SoD analysis, rulesets, mitigating controls, emergency access and review of privileged activity. For Fiori, I need to understand that what a user sees in the launchpad and what the backend authorizes are related but not identical.

For changes, I ask how a change moves from development through testing and approval into production. For interfaces and jobs, I ask what happens when processing fails and how completeness is monitored. For reports used in controls, I ask how the population is proven complete and accurate. For RISE and cloud services, I ask which responsibilities remain with the customer.

My most useful technical phrase is often simple: show me. Show me the approval. Show me the role. Show me the log. Show me the reconciliation. Show me what happens when it fails. I use technical literacy to ask better questions, not to pretend I am the specialist.
reviewQuestions: What is the control objective behind the technical explanation?
What would I ask the SME to show me?
What evidence would support the answer?
What red flag would cause escalation?
Do I need a specialist before concluding?

connect.nowKnow: I can ask stronger technical questions and recognize red flags.
connect.stillNeed: I still need to control the flow of requests, evidence and questions with auditors.
connect.buildNext: Build the Audit Request and Resolution Dashboard.

activities.scenario: Specialists tell you that access, transports, interfaces, reports and RISE responsibilities are controlled. You must determine what to ask and what to see.

activities.title: Module 5 — Managing Internal and External Audit
activities.narration:
An audit request is not complete because someone attached a file. Before evidence leaves the controls team, I need to know that it answers the request and supports the control.

I log each request, assign an internal owner, confirm the due date and identify what the auditor is actually trying to prove. When evidence arrives, the team performs quality review before submission. If the evidence is wrong, incomplete or for the wrong period, I return it internally rather than sending a weak package to the auditor.

When the auditor asks a follow-up question, I separate a request for clarification from a genuine control exception. If management disagrees with an auditor conclusion, I bring the discussion back to the control objective, the evidence and the facts.

I also manage the relationship. I do not hide problems, and I do not concede unsupported conclusions. I communicate early when deadlines are at risk. I keep an audit trail of what was requested, what was submitted, what was questioned and how the matter was resolved.

My role is to make the audit process controlled, factual and efficient.
reviewQuestions: Does the evidence actually answer the audit request?
Was it quality-reviewed before submission?
Is this a clarification or a genuine exception?
What is overdue and who owns it?
What should be escalated now?

connect.nowKnow: I can manage audit requests and evidence quality.
connect.stillNeed: I still need to turn exceptions into risk decisions, remediation and closure.
connect.buildNext: Build the Deficiency and Remediation Register.

activities.title: Module 6 — Deficiencies, Remediation and Risk Decisions
activities.narration:
Finding an exception is only the beginning. I need to understand what failed, why it failed and what risk that failure creates.

I first connect the issue back to the control objective and the underlying risk. I determine whether the exception is isolated or whether it indicates a broader problem. I look for root cause rather than accepting a superficial explanation.

If a compensating control exists, I ask whether it genuinely reduces the same risk and whether it operated effectively. I identify the remediation owner, the action required and a realistic target date. I also decide who needs to know now rather than waiting for the next status meeting.

A remediation item is not closed because management says it is fixed. The change must be implemented and, where appropriate, retested. Closure evidence must support the conclusion.

My responsibility is to make sure deficiencies become managed decisions rather than entries that sit indefinitely in a spreadsheet.
reviewQuestions: What failed and which risk does it expose?
Is the issue isolated or systemic?
Is the proposed compensating control valid?
Is remediation specific, owned and dated?
What evidence will be required to close it?

connect.nowKnow: I can evaluate deficiencies and govern remediation.
connect.stillNeed: I still need to translate detailed project information into executive decisions.

activities.scenario: Testing identifies several exceptions. One appears isolated; another may affect multiple business units. Management wants to know what is serious and what must happen next.

activities.title: Module 7 — Executive Communication and Governance
activities.narration:
Executives do not need me to read the workpapers to them. They need to know whether the controls program is under control, where the important risks are and what decisions they need to make.

I reduce the detail into a small number of management measures: scope confirmation, control coverage, testing progress, overdue evidence, significant deficiencies, remediation status and decisions required.

For every major issue I answer the same questions. What happened? Why does it matter? What are we doing about it? Who owns the action? When will it be resolved? What decision or support do I need?

I also change my language for the audience. With an analyst I can discuss detailed testing steps. With a control owner I focus on the business risk and the action required. With the CFO or CIO I focus on exposure, impact, accountability, timing and decisions.

Good executive communication is not removing important information. It is organizing the important information so management can act.

connect.nowKnow: I can communicate program health and decisions to executives.
connect.stillNeed: I now need to integrate all leadership skills under realistic time pressure.

activities.title: Module 8 — First 30 Days as Controls Lead or Manager — Capstone
activities.narration:
This capstone is different from the foundation course. I am no longer being tested on whether I can personally complete every workbook. I am being tested on whether I can take accountability for the program.

During Week One I take control. I meet the sponsor and team, assess the fourteen artifacts, review prior findings, establish governance, build the RACI and issue assignments. By Friday I must give management a reliable status.

During Week Two I direct and challenge. I review analyst work, question SAP specialists, resolve evidence problems, manage auditor requests and adjust resources when work falls behind.

During Week Three I review and decide. I assess testing results, reject weak workpapers, evaluate deficiencies, meet control owners, agree remediation and escalate important risks.

During Week Four I govern and lead. I finalize the executive dashboard, run the remediation and steering meetings, present the thirty-day assessment and propose the sixty- and ninety-day roadmap.

The standard is simple. Can I explain what is happening, prove the status, assign the right people, detect weak work, make defensible decisions and take accountability for the outcome? That is the transition from building the controls project to leading it.
reviewQuestions: Did I establish control of the program in Week One?
Did I delegate rather than absorb the team's work?
Did I detect weak work and technical gaps?
Did I manage audit and remediation effectively?
Can I defend my 30/60/90-day plan to the sponsor?

connect.nowKnow: I have practiced taking accountability for an inherited controls program.
connect.stillNeed: I must continue applying the same leadership disciplines on real projects.
connect.buildNext: Own the controls program: direct, challenge, review, decide and govern.
